extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers wanting to write a novella
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for planning, drafting, structuring, editing, and publishing a novella — the mid-length fiction form between a short story and a novel. Covers word-count definitions, plotting methods, character economy, pacing, unity, and publication options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-count definition of a novella
rubrics_metrics.description: A novella is longer than a short story but shorter than a novel; McEwan suggests 'something... between twenty and forty thousand words.' The Science Fiction and Fantasy Writers of America (Nebula Awards) define novella as 17,500–40,000 words. Writer's Relief notes the exact limit isn't set in stone and suggests 30,000–60,000 words may be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide which range you adopt as your target; be aware different publishers/awards use different thresholds. Shorter inspirational novellas may fall below some ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lean architecture — cut excess
rubrics_metrics.description: Novellas demand cutting away all excess fat to leave something lean and appetizing; the central idea must dominate the structure rather than digressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan with strict economy: remove scenes/lines that do not serve the main idea. Use the novella's length to hold a whole structure clearly in a reader's mind; avoid the rambling or bloated feeling of an under-edited novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use characters economically
rubrics_metrics.description: Because space is limited, novellas typically have a trimmer cast. Identify the crucial contribution each character makes to the story and theme and give each character only enough dialogue and description to further the plot and create vividness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat roles like actors with limited lines: determine whether each character helps or hinders the protagonist and pare back backstory or surplus detail. Example: Fahrenheit 451's central cast of ~10 people with varying development levels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit changes in setting
rubrics_metrics.description: Novellas are likely to have fewer changes in setting than novels; avoid many location shifts that consume word count without advancing the central idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you use multiple locations, avoid spending space explaining transit or logistics; favor settings that support the central conflict and voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep a clear central idea in focus
rubrics_metrics.description: The novella should have a clear central idea that 'is always exerting its gravitational pull' so that all elements orbit that idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At every page turn ask: How does this scene fit into my central idea? Ensure scenes, motifs and character choices reinforce that core concept rather than distract.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single central conflict
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlike many novels, a novella usually has one single conflict (which can be internal) rather than multiple subplots that complicate the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The central conflict should be complex enough to sustain the length but resolvable within the word-count limits. It should rise in stakes/anticipation over the first two thirds and be resolved in the final third.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arc planning — three-scene/three-part structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Novellas can be planned around a concise arc (example: Fahrenheit 451's three-scene arc: establishment of central idea and relationships; broadening the cast and resistance; intensifying conflict and resolution).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a tight three-part or three-scene plan to ensure momentum and clarity: exposition/establishment, complication/development, intensifying conflict and resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plot points to map action
rubrics_metrics.description: Outline using plot points — discrete events that drive the narrative forward — and map them visually (e.g., graphing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly-cited plot points include: Exposition (hook/inciting action), First plot point, First pinch point, Midpoint, Final pinch point, Final plot point (all appears lost), Resolution. Adapt or reorder as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify the problem and the solution (know your end point)
rubrics_metrics.description: When outlining or taking notes, identify the core problem/conflict and have a clear idea of the solution or end point, even if you prefer to discover the story while writing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writing a one-line blurb or using the snowflake method's initial sentence can help clarify the problem and endpoint; knowing the destination improves focus and coherence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Snowflake method as an outlining option
rubrics_metrics.description: The snowflake method (Randy Ingermanson) is a 10-step planning process beginning with a one-sentence summary and expanding to synopsis, characters and scenes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the snowflake if you prefer extensive planning before drafting; it helps scale an idea up into a workable novella structure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use character-development guides / bibles
rubrics_metrics.description: Compile character dossiers or a character bible (names, motivations, backstory details) to compress necessary detail efficiently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: military-style dossiers listing nationality, birth, occupation, motivations and concise indicators of temperament. Use spreadsheets or the site’s character outlining system to keep development focused and economical.

rubrics_metrics.name: 25-scene rule and approximate scene length
rubrics_metrics.description: One practical plotting heuristic: estimate ~1,000 words per scene. Thus, a 25,000-word novella might have ~25 scenes (and a 40,000-word one ~40 scenes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether to write in numbered scenes or chapter-like sections; use scene counts to pace rising action and ensure even development across the novella.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase pace — prune subplots and use concision
rubrics_metrics.description: Novellas should move briskly: prune subplots, use shorter sentences and outline-like concision to maintain forward momentum toward the climax.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stop-start scenic detours typical of novels. Ensure each sentence and scene serves movement toward the climax; keep tension building rather than letting the narrative meander.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observe the classical unities (time, place, action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use three unities to keep the story compact: unity of time (limited frame), unity of place (one main location or limited locations), and unity of action (a simple, easily resolved conflict).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applying these unities helps limit scope and forces focus on the central story; multiple locations are acceptable but avoid spending words on transit or exposition about moving between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flash-linked novella approach
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a novella as a series of linked flash pieces (~1,000 words each) with a shared thread (location, motif, or recurring event) that together form a cohesive arc (examples: The House on Mango Street; Dept. of Speculation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method allows experimental structure and vignette-driven storytelling while maintaining a unifying element that binds the pieces into a novella-length work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit with ruthless precision
rubrics_metrics.description: In a shorter work, every page is more visible; edit to ensure each page contributes to the whole and eliminate passages that bore or are overly wordy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At each page: ask 'How does this scene fit into my central idea? What reason have I given the reader to turn to the next page?' Trim or rework scenes that don't advance theme, character or plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication options and positioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Novellas have different receptivity across markets: genre publishers are often more receptive than literary ones; options include traditional genre publishers, literary journals that accept novellas, self-publishing (e.g., Kindle), publishing a novella alongside stories, or bundling multiple novellas in one volume.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research publishers and competitions that accept novellas (lists recommended). Consider format and audience when submitting: genre readers may prefer standalone novellas, while literary markets may expect a particular tone or experimental form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enter novella competitions and seek appropriate markets
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep an eye out for novella-specific competitions (including flash-novella contests) and lists of journals/publishers that accept novellas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions and targeted publisher lists can help place a novella; match your novella's form (genre, literary, flash-linked) to receptive outlets.
